stories.summary: Lundy made its name on voice AI for real estate — voice search, a voice app for adding and editing listings, Navigator, an assistant trained on listing-database rules that answers questions at help desks, and nora, its agent assistant, which MetroList rolled out to more than 20,000 subscribers in June. On November 3 it shipped Jefe, a voice assistant for every agent at LoKation Real Estate, a six-state brokerage based in Pompano Beach, Florida. Jefe carries LoKation's name, Lundy builds and maintains it, and it was designed with LoKation's leaders around how the brokerage actually works. The point: the company that used to sell to the listing databases now sells straight to the brokerage, and its tool sits on top of the systems they already use instead of replacing them.
stories.title: Lundy sells its first assistant to a big brokerage — the listing-database vendor crosses over

stories.summary: RealtyMark, a Philadelphia-area independent brokerage with more than 2,000 agents across eight states, launched a new company platform at realtymark.net, built on Smart Agent Guide. Every agent has been live on it since October 30. Up front is AImee, the company's AI helper, answering the website chat and phone around the clock in more than 25 languages and sending each lead to the right agent. Same pattern as the Lundy story, from the other direction — a mid-size independent brokerage buying a whole AI platform (website, customer system, and AI helper) in one purchase, instead of piecing tools together agent by agent.
stories.title: RealtyMark puts 2,000 agents on one AI platform — a mid-size brokerage buys the whole thing at once

stories.summary: Cotality's CoreAI is the smart layer running through more than 210 of its products. Its MCP Server — a standard plug, launched March 31 — lets any AI assistant connect once, see which data it's allowed to use, and pull answers in real time: property details, climate risk, ownership, market trends. It's the model for Jessica's pitch, and it just won an award: the data owner sets the terms, the assistant only sees what it's allowed to see, and the broker's name stays attached to the data.
stories.title: Cotality lets AI in through the front door — and wins an award for it

stories.summary: Draper Goren Blockchain Studio launched LenDb.ai, a free directory of 224,703 US mortgage loan officers — 48,228 full profiles built from 721 lenders' own loan-officer pages, 512,101 license records across all 50 states, DC, and the territories — made for the way people now shop for a mortgage: by asking an AI assistant. The company says it's run day to day by an AI chief executive answering to a human board — that's their claim, not verified. It's the same shape JJ tracks in his open-data thread: a big public dataset packaged as a free feed for AI assistants, handed out through the directory where AI assistants find tools to plug into instead of a website.
stories.title: LenDb.ai: a free loan-officer directory built for AI assistants

hook: The company that used to sell to the listing databases now sells straight to the brokerages — and its tool plugs into the systems they already use instead of replacing them.
market_map: Today: a voice-AI company sells its first assistant to a big brokerage; a 2,000-agent brokerage buys one AI platform for everyone; the property-data giant wins an award for letting AI in through the front door; and a free loan-officer directory built for AI assistants.
one_line: One AI helper for the independent brokerage — whatever system it already runs on.

openings.text: Every launch this week runs on one company's system — Jefe on BoldTrail, AImee on Smart Agent Guide, Aly inside Cotality's Araya. But a 2,000-agent independent brokerage that doesn't use BoldTrail has no ready-made AI helper that plugs into the customer system and listing database it already has. That gap — one helper, any system, with the brokerage's own rules and fair-housing checks built in — is the opening that lasts no matter which platform wins.
openings.title: One AI helper for the independent brokerage, whatever system it runs on

watch.text: The final approval hearing was Monday, November 2, at 9:30 AM, before Judge Jenkins in Illinois. No ruling has surfaced as of this morning. Don't cite approval. One November 2 newsletter writes as if approval is only a matter of time — that's the author's guess, not a ruling.

watch.text: The next step is still the motion to dismiss — the request to throw the case out before trial — with no trial date set. No news from San Francisco's MLS — the open questions haven't changed.
watch.title: Compass fight quiet

watch.text: The FTC ordered nine companies to hand over details on personalized pricing (45 days to respond; comments on the enforcement plan end November 21). The FTC and seven states sued Toast on October 29, and the Riverside Payments settlement (November 2, a $32.1M judgment suspended after a $600K payment) — hidden-fee and hard-to-cancel enforcement is now a pattern in business software, not just consumer apps.
